claim: Prime editing is a recently developed CRISPR/Cas9 based gene engineering tool that allows the introduction of short insertions, deletions, and substitutions into the genome.
source: Prime editing is a recently developed CRISPR/Cas9 based gene engineering tool that allows the introduction of short insertions, deletions, and substitutions into the genome.
evidence: This is a general characterization of prime editing technology, supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: The efficiency of prime editing typically achieves editing rates of around 10%–30%.
source: However, the efficiency of prime editing, which typically achieves editing rates of around 10%–30%, has not matched its versatility.
evidence: This is stated as a known characteristic of prime editing efficiency.

claim: PEAR has no background fluorescence and specifically indicates prime editing events.
source: PEAR has no background fluorescence and specifically indicates prime editing events.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E demonstrating specificity.

claim: PEAR provides apparently unlimited flexibility for sequence variation along the entire length of the spacer sequence.
source: Its design provides apparently unlimited flexibility for sequence variation along the entire length of the spacer sequence, making it uniquely suited for systematic investigation of sequence features that influence prime editing activity.
evidence: This is supported by the design shown in Figure 1A and experimental validation in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: The use of PEAR as an enrichment marker for prime editing can increase the edited population by up to 84%.
source: The use of PEAR as an enrichment marker for prime editing can increase the edited population by up to 84%, thus significantly improving the applicability of prime editing for basic research and biotechnological applications.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Many CRISPR-based approaches rely on generating double-stranded DNA breaks that are usually accompanied by genome-wide off-target editing.
source: Many of the CRISPR-based approaches rely on generating double-stranded DNA breaks that are usually accompanied by genome-wide off-target editing (Tsai et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2015; Kleinstiver et al., 2016b; Tsai et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Base and prime editors can introduce modifications into the DNA with a base pair resolution without the requirement of donor DNA templates or the introduction of double-stranded DNA breaks.
source: Recently, more precise CRISPR tools—base (Komor et al., 2016; Gaudelli et al., 2017) and prime (Anzalone et al., 2019) editors—have been developed, and these enzymes can introduce modifications into the DNA with a base pair resolution without the requirement of donor DNA templates or the introduction of double-stranded DNA breaks.
evidence: This is supported by citations to the original publications describing these technologies.

claim: Current base editor variants provide efficient editing but are restricted to certain substitution mutations.
source: While current base editor (BE) variants provide efficient editing, they are restricted to certain substitution mutations (Komor et al., 2016; Gaudelli et al., 2017; Kurt et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on base editors.

claim: Prime editors can introduce all types of substitutions and/or precise insertions/deletions (indels), however, their efficiency lags behind that of base editors.
source: In contrast, prime editors (PEs) can introduce all types of substitutions and/or precise insertions/deletions (indels), however, their efficiency lags behind that of BEs.
evidence: This is a comparison based on established knowledge of the two technologies.

claim: Prime editor 2 (PE2) consists of a nickase version of Streptococcus pyogenes Cas9 (SpCas9) fused to a reverse transcriptase enzyme.
source: Prime editor 2 (PE2) consists of a nickase version of Streptococcus pyogenes Cas9 (SpCas9) fused to a reverse transcriptase enzyme (Anzalone et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a description of PE2 architecture supported by citation to the original publication.

claim: The fused reverse transcriptase can extend the nicked DNA strand using an RNA template that is located on the 3′ terminus of an extended single-guide RNA (sgRNA), called the prime editing sgRNA (pegRNA).
source: The fused reverse transcriptase can extend the nicked DNA strand using an RNA template that is located on the 3′ terminus of an extended single-guide RNA (sgRNA), called the prime editing sgRNA (pegRNA).
evidence: This describes the mechanism of prime editing based on established knowledge.

claim: The optimal length of the PBS and the RT varies from target to target and requires extensive optimization for each different target.
source: The optimal length of the PBS and the RT varies from target to target and requires extensive optimization for each different target.
evidence: This is supported by the optimization experiments shown in Figures 1B and 2.

claim: The efficiency of prime editing can be increased by nicking the non-edited strand (prime editor 3—PE3) at the expense of potentially generating unwanted indels at the targeted locus.
source: The efficiency of prime editing can be increased by nicking the non-edited strand (prime editor 3—PE3) at the expense of potentially generating unwanted indels at the targeted locus (Anzalone et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the original PE publication and confirmed by data in Figures 1B and 2.

claim: Altering the PAM sequence with the desired mutation may prevent the PE from nicking the sequence again, which can reduce the chance of introducing unwanted indels alongside the intended mutations.
source: In some cases, the efficiency of prime editing can be further increased by also altering the PAM sequence with the desired mutation this may prevent the PE from nicking the sequence again. This method can reduce the chance of introducing unwanted indels alongside the intended mutations, thus increasing the occurrence of precise modifications (Anzalone et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the original PE publication.

claim: Several systems have been developed for reporting base editing that use BEs for the generation or alteration of a start or stop codon.
source: Several systems have been developed for reporting base editing that use BEs for the generation or alteration of a start or stop codon (Katti et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020), or to rescue a disruptive amino acid and subsequently recover functions of antibiotic resistance genes or fluorescence proteins (Martin et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on base editing reporters.

claim: A non-synonymous mutation in the chromophore of a fluorescent protein that induces fluorescence spectral change has been explored as a method to monitor base editing activity.
source: Alternatively, a non-synonymous mutation in the chromophore of a fluorescent protein that induces fluorescence spectral change has also been explored as a method to monitor base editing activity (Coelho et al., 2018; Standage-Beier et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Reporter systems for prime editing were restricted to very few target sequences and/or showed a rather low signal.
source: Reporter systems have also been demonstrated for prime editing, but they were restricted to very few target sequences (Lin et al., 2020; Sürün et al., 2020) and/or showed a rather low signal (Katti et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on prime editing reporters.

claim: Prime edited mammalian cells can be identified and enriched by using a plasmid-based surrogate marker for chromosomal DNA modifications, as demonstrated before with Cas nucleases and base editors.
source: We also wanted to find out whether prime edited mammalian cells could be identified and enriched by using a plasmid-based surrogate marker for chromosomal DNA modifications, as demonstrated before with Cas nucleases (Ramakrishna et al., 2014; Grav et al., 2015) and BEs (Katti et al., 2020; Coelho et al., 2018; St Martin et al., 2018; Tálas et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and confirmed by experimental data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: BEAR is based on a split GFP protein separated by the last intron of the mouse Vim gene.
source: BEAR is based on a split GFP protein separated by the last intron of the mouse Vim gene.
evidence: This is a description of the BEAR system design, supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In BEAR, the sequence of the functional splice donor site is altered in such way that splicing and therefore the GFP fluorescence is disrupted, however, they can be restored by applying adenine or cytosine base editors.
source: The sequence of the functional splice donor site (or 5′ splice site) is altered in such way, that splicing and therefore the GFP fluorescence is disrupted, however, they can be restored by applying adenine or cytosine BEs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the description and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Sequence alterations in the intronic sequence of BEAR are well tolerated, which provides flexibility to investigate numerous target sequences.
source: Sequence alterations in the intronic sequence are well tolerated, which gave us the flexibility to investigate numerous target sequences.
evidence: This is based on previous work with BEAR cited in the manuscript.

claim: PEAR contains an inactive splice site which can be activated by the action of a PE harboring an appropriately designed pegRNA.
source: Using the information acquired during the development of the BEAR system (Tálas et al., 2021), we have designed a plasmid that contains an inactive splice site, which can be activated by the action of a PE harboring an appropriately designed pegRNA (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the description and Figure 1A showing the design.

claim: Cells containing plasmids with activated splice site sequences will be able to efficiently express GFP, which can be quantified by flow cytometry.
source: Cells containing plasmids with activated splice site sequences will then be able to efficiently express GFP, which can be quantified by flow cytometry.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown throughout the manuscript using flow cytometry.

claim: The editing windows of base editors exploited for the BEAR system are located PAM distal, 5′ of the nick.
source: The editing windows of BEs exploited for the BEAR system are located PAM distal, 5′ of the nick (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1B showing the BEAR design.

claim: Prime editors can introduce mutations 3′ of the nick, a region that contains the PAM sequence.
source: PEs on the other hand can introduce mutations 3′ of the nick, a region that contains the PAM sequence (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by Figures 1A and 1—figure supplement 1C showing the PEAR design.

claim: In PEAR, the target sequence can be freely adjusted in its entire length because the PAM is placed on the complementary strand.
source: To ensure maximum flexibility for the PE target, we kept the target sequence in the intron by placing the PAM to the complementary strand. As a result, the target sequence can be freely adjusted in its entire length (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the design shown in Figure 1A and experimental validation in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: PEAR is similar to BEAR in that it is permissive with respect to the interchangeability of the targeted nucleotides.
source: Thus, while BEAR could be used with a few million of different target sequences, PEAR offers unrestricted sequence variations for the entire SpCas9 target. On the contrary, PEAR is similar to BEAR in that it is permissive with respect to the interchangeability of the targeted nucleotides (here the splice site and the splice site flanking nucleotides; Tálas et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and experimental data in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: No other fluorescence-based reporter systems have demonstrated the degree of flexibility shown by PEAR.
source: No other fluorescence-based reporter systems have demonstrated such degree of flexibility before (Katti et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2020; Sürün et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a comparative claim supported by citations to other reporter systems.

claim: The PEAR-GFP plasmid can be efficiently edited by many combinations of PBS, RT, and nicking position.
source: The heatmap in Figure 1B shows that the PEAR-GFP plasmid can be efficiently edited by many of these combinations of PBS, RT, and nicking position.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The most efficient editing of PEAR-GFP occurred when a 10-nucleotide long PBS (PBS-10) and a 24-nucleotide long RT region (RT-24) were applied.
source: The most efficient editing occurred, when a 10-nucleotide long PBS (PBS-10) and a 24-nucleotide long RT region (RT-24) were applied.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Editing efficiency is generally higher when the complementary strand is nicked than when it is not.
source: Figure 1B also shows that in line with expectations, editing efficiency is generally higher when the complementary strand is nicked, than when it is not (Anzalone et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data in Figure 1B and citation to the original PE publication.

claim: The most effective complementary strand nicking site was position +17 in the case of most PBS and RT length combinations.
source: The most effective complementary strand nicking site was position +17 in the case of most PBS and RT length combinations.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In all conditions, PBS-10 gave greater values than PBS-13 and PBS-16.
source: In all conditions, PBS-10 gave greater values than PBS-13 and PBS-16.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Comparing the RTs, the efficiency of the editing was in the order of RT-24>RT-33>RT-16 in most conditions (16 out of 18).
source: Comparing the RTs, the efficiency of the editing was in the order of RT-24>RT-33>RT-16 in most conditions (16 out of 18).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The effect of the length of PBS and RT on editing efficiency is primarily independent of one another.
source: These results are consistent with the concept that the effect of the length of PBS and RT on editing efficiency is primarily independent of one another (Kim et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data in Figure 1B and citation to published research.

claim: PE efficiency is governed by the same factors when using a PEAR plasmid as demonstrated earlier on chromosomal targets.
source: Thus, these experiments support the hypothesis, that PE efficiency is governed by the same factors when using a PEAR plasmid, as demonstrated earlier on chromosomal targets (Anzalone et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data in Figures 1B and 2, and citations to published research.

claim: PEAR specifically reports on prime editing activity and is insensitive to the potential presence of indel background.
source: As expected, while all three variants—SpCas9 nuclease, nickase, or PE—demonstrated GFP disruption activity, only PE restored mScarlet fluorescence, indicating that PEAR specifically reports on prime editing activity and is insensitive to the potential presence of indel background (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: All types of sequence alterations (insertions, deletions, substitutions) can be examined using the PEAR system.
source: Figure 1C demonstrates that all types of sequence alterations can be examined using the PEAR system.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: There seems to be no connection between the efficiency and the complexity of the editing in PEAR.
source: Interestingly, there seems to be no connection between the efficiency and the complexity of the editing.
evidence: This is an observation based on the experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The versatility of the PEAR assay lies in the fact that an active splice site can be restored from seemingly any inactive sequence as long as the change can be efficiently implemented by prime editing.
source: The versatility of the PEAR assay, with respect to sequence modifications, lies not only in the fact that an active splice site can be restored from seemingly any inactive sequence as long as the change can be efficiently implemented by prime editing, but also that the active splice site sequence itself can be varied.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: The active splice site sequence itself can be varied in PEAR.
source: The versatility of the PEAR assay, with respect to sequence modifications, lies not only in the fact that an active splice site can be restored from seemingly any inactive sequence as long as the change can be efficiently implemented by prime editing, but also that the active splice site sequence itself can be varied. To demonstrate this, we corrected three additional active splice sites from different inactive sequences (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The same factors influence prime editing on a plasmid as on genomic targets.
source: In order to verify that the same factors influence prime editing on a plasmid as on genomic targets, we compared prime editing efficiency on previously constructed plasmids and two HEK293T cell lines (HEK-BEAR-GFP and HEK-BEAR-mScarlet—Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Tálas et al., 2021) that contain a chromosomal copy of these plasmids harboring an interrupted GFP or mScarlet sequence, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: For BEAR-GFP, PBS-13 and RT-22 or RT-26 in combination with the second nick site at position +103 results in maximum efficiency for both the plasmid and the cell line.
source: The heatmap in Figure 2A shows that PBS-13 and RT-22 or RT-26 in combination with the second nick site at position +103 results in maximum efficiency for the BEAR-GFP plasmid. In the absence of a second nick, the efficiency of editing was considerably lower. The most ideal conditions for prime editing were the same both in the plasmid and in the cell line (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The overall pattern of prime editing efficiency between the BEAR-GFP plasmid and cell line is similar, exhibiting strong correlation (r=0.89).
source: The overall pattern of the two heatmaps is indisputably similar, exhibiting strong correlation (r=0.89, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data and correlation analysis shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: In the case of the cell line, a somewhat lower general editing efficiency is apparent compared to that with the plasmid, likely due to the much higher copy number of the plasmids present in the cell.
source: In case of the cell line, a somewhat lower general editing efficiency is apparent compared to that with the plasmid. This difference is likely due to the much higher copy number of the plasmids present in the cell.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: For mScarlet target 1, the top working PBS is 10 nucleotides long in the case of both the BEAR-mScarlet plasmid and the cell line.
source: Target 1 gave higher prime editing efficiencies, with the top working PBS being 10 nucleotides long in the case of both the BEAR-mScarlet plasmid and the cell line (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The two heatmaps for mScarlet target 1 exhibit a remarkably similar pattern, with a strong correlation of the editing efficiency in the cell line and the BEAR plasmid (r=0.93).
source: The two heatmaps exhibit a remarkably similar pattern, and there is a strong correlation of the editing efficiency in the cell line and the BEAR plasmid (r=0.93; Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data and correlation analysis shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: For mScarlet target 2, the best PBS length is also 10 nucleotides long for both the BEAR-mScarlet plasmid and the cell line.
source: Similar outcomes can be seen with target 2 where the best PBS length is also 10 nucleotides long for both the BEAR-mScarlet plasmid and the cell line (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Comparing plasmid and genomic results for mScarlet target 2 revealed a remarkably similar pattern (r=0.92).
source: Comparing plasmid and genomic results also revealed a remarkably similar pattern (r=0.92; Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data and correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B and 2D.

claim: For all three targets studied, regardless of whether in plasmids or in cell lines, the three secondary nick positions affected the effectiveness of prime editing in the same way.
source: For all three targets studied, regardless of whether in plasmids or in cell lines, the three secondary nick positions affected the effectiveness of prime editing in the same way.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The main features of prime editing and factors affecting its efficiency are reflected accurately within the PEAR system.
source: Collectively, these results strongly imply that the main features of prime editing and factors affecting its efficiency are reflected accurately within our system.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Post-transfection selection of edited cells by FACS or antibiotics have proven to be effective methods for the enrichment of genetically modified cells within a population.
source: Post-transfection selection of edited cells by fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) or antibiotics have proven to be effective methods for the enrichment of genetically modified cells within a population, given that the SpCas9 coding plasmid co-expressed a protein that is fluorescent or bears antibiotic resistance (Katti et al., 2020; Standage-Beier et al., 2019; Ramakrishna et al., 2014; Grav et al., 2015; St Martin et al., 2018; Tálas et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Selecting for cells with a surrogate marker that is subjected to the same type of genetic modification as the intended edit results in higher enrichment of successfully edited cells than when solely selecting for transfection markers.
source: Experiments have also shown that selecting for cells with a surrogate marker, that is subjected to the same type of genetic modification (knockout, HDR, or base editing) as the intended edit, results in higher enrichment of successfully edited cells, than when solely selecting for transfection markers (Katti et al., 2020; Coelho et al., 2018; Ramakrishna et al., 2014; Grav et al., 2015; St Martin et al., 2018; Tálas et al., 2021; Yan et al., 2020) suggesting that some individual cells allow for higher editing efficiency.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research and confirmed by experimental data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Some individual cells allow for higher editing efficiency, which could be due to the nuclease being able to exhibit higher activity, or the activity of DNA repair systems being considerably more engaged in these cells.
source: Experiments have also shown that selecting for cells with a surrogate marker, that is subjected to the same type of genetic modification (knockout, HDR, or base editing) as the intended edit, results in higher enrichment of successfully edited cells, than when solely selecting for transfection markers (Katti et al., 2020; Coelho et al., 2018; Ramakrishna et al., 2014; Grav et al., 2015; St Martin et al., 2018; Tálas et al., 2021; Yan et al., 2020) suggesting that some individual cells allow for higher editing efficiency. This phenomenon could be due to the nuclease being able to exhibit higher activity, or the activity of DNA repair systems could be considerably more engaged in these cells.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed enrichment phenomenon.

claim: Transfection marker enrichments significantly increased the ratio of edited and non-edited cells: gating for the BFP-expressing cells increased the percentage of the edited population from 18% to 24% with both pegRNAs tested.
source: Figure 3A shows that transfection marker enrichments significantly increased the ratio of edited and non-edited cells: gating for the BFP-expressing cells increased the percentage of the edited population from 18% to 24% with both pegRNAs tested.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: PEAR-enrichment resulted in a considerable increase compared to the transfection enrichments, with 57% and 76% mScarlet expressing cells for the two pegRNAs tested.
source: PEAR-enrichment resulted in a considerable increase compared to the transfection enrichments in case of both pegRNAs (57% and 76% mScarlet expressing cells, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Prime edited cells can be substantially enriched when using a PEAR plasmid as a surrogate marker.
source: These results demonstrate that prime edited cells can be substantially enriched when using a PEAR plasmid as a surrogate marker.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: PEAR enrichments ranged between about twofold and fourfold, reaching up to 62% and 76% editing at FANCF site in K562 and HEK293T cells, respectively.
source: PEAR enrichments ranged between about twofold and fourfold, reaching up to 62% and 76% editing at FANCF site in K562 and HEK293T cells, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Editing the FANCF target in HUES9 cells showed a 7.8-fold increase with 28% PEAR-enriched editing, whilst editing without enrichment remained below 4% in HUES9 cells.
source: Editing the same target in HUES9 cells showed a 7.8-fold increase with 28% PEAR-enriched editing, whilst editing without enrichment remained below 4% in HUES9 cells (Figure 3C and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Enrichments increased the incidence of indels at the edited sites in the population in 8 out of the 13 edits.
source: Enrichments increased the incidence of indels at the edited sites in the population in 8 out of the 13 edits.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The extent of indel increments is generally low: the specificity slightly decreased for only one edit, while it slightly increased in five cases.
source: However, the extent of these increments is generally low: the specificity slightly decreased for only one edit, while it slightly increased in five cases (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Only 1 of the 15 off-target sites showed detectable editing and indel formation that was also enriched by PEAR enrichments.
source: Only 1 of the 15 off-target sites showed detectable editing (Figure 3F) and indel formation (Figure 3G) that was also enriched by PEAR enrichments.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figures 3F and 3G.

claim: For the remaining 14 off-target sites, PEAR-enrichment did not increase either off-target editing or indel formation to a detectable level.
source: For the remaining 14 sites, PEAR-enrichment did not increase either off-target editing or indel formation to a detectable level.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figures 3F and 3G.

claim: PEAR enrichments substantially increase prime editing in various cell lines without compromising neither on-target nor off-target specificity.
source: Thus, these data suggest that PEAR enrichments substantially increase prime editing in various cell lines without compromising neither on-target nor off-target specificity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data shown in Figures 3C-G.

claim: Integration of the active PEAR plasmid to the genome is minimal.
source: Figure 3—figure supplement 1 shows that integration of the active plasmid to the genome is minimal; however, since plasmids tend to integrate into the genome, albeit with low efficiency, unedited PEAR plasmids are likely to still integrate into the genome.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Unedited PEAR plasmids are likely to still integrate into the genome, albeit with low efficiency.
source: Figure 3—figure supplement 1 shows that integration of the active plasmid to the genome is minimal; however, since plasmids tend to integrate into the genome, albeit with low efficiency, unedited PEAR plasmids are likely to still integrate into the genome.
evidence: This is an inference based on known plasmid behavior and the data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Clones should be checked for the absence of the transfected plasmids, such as the PE-expressing and the PEAR plasmid.
source: Clones should be checked for the absence of the transfected plasmids, such as the PE-expressing and the PEAR plasmid.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the potential for plasmid integration.

claim: The pegRNA used for co-editing the PEAR plasmid should have no on-target site in the genome and have only minimal genome-wide off-target effect in order to decrease the potential off-target events during PEAR-enrichments.
source: It is also important, that the pegRNA used for co-editing the PEAR plasmid has no on-target site in the genome and has only minimal genome-wide off-target effect in order to decrease the potential off-target events during PEAR-enrichments.
evidence: This is a design consideration for optimal use of PEAR.

claim: Both EGFP site 2 and EGFP site 7 sgRNAs have no detectable off-targets as assessed by GUIDE-seq.
source: The genome-wide off-target sites of WT-SpCas9 nuclease for EGFP site 2 have been determined previously (Kulcsár et al., 2020) and for EGFP site 7, they were determined in this work by GUIDE-seq. Both sgRNAs proved to have no detectable off-targets (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by GUIDE-seq data shown in Figure 4A and citation to previous work.

claim: The highest editing was found with EGFP site 2 with a 12-nucleotide long PBS sequence.
source: The highest editing was found with EGFP site 2 with a 12-nucleotide long PBS sequence.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The PEAR-GFP-2in1-2.0 plasmid is suitable for the enrichment of prime editing and confirmed the efficiency of PEAR-enrichment for various types of editing.
source: This plasmid—named PEAR-GFP-2in1-2.0—was used in subsequent experiments to enrich additional nine target sites installing three insertions, deletions, and substitutions each (Figure 4C–E). These results proved that the PEAR-GFP-2in1-2.0 plasmid is also suitable for the enrichment of prime editing and confirmed the efficiency of PEAR-enrichment for various types of editing.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figures 4C-E.

claim: The editing rates by PEAR-enrichments increased from 2.1- to 4.6-fold and up to 84%.
source: The editing rates by PEAR-enrichments increased from 2.1- to 4.6-fold and up to 84% (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The increase in editing rates is not accompanied with a decrease in specificity in the case of any of the nine target sites tested with PEAR-GFP-2in1-2.0.
source: Figure 4D and E show that the increase in editing rates is not accompanied with a decrease in specificity in the case of any of the nine target sites.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figures 4D and 4E.

claim: Prime editing technology has readily been translated from mammalian models to plants and Drosophila.
source: Prime editing technology has readily been translated from mammalian models (Anzalone et al., 2019; Sürün et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020; Schene et al., 2020) to plants (Lin et al., 2020; Jiang et al., 2020; Lu et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2020) and Drosophila (Bosch et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: During the preparation of the manuscript, surprisingly few studies had demonstrated the practical use of prime editing in mammalian cells.
source: Despite its great potential, during the preparation of our manuscript, we have found surprisingly few studies that had demonstrated the practical use of prime editing in mammalian cells (Sürün et al., 2020; Schene et al., 2020), which is a vast underestimation of the true potential flexibility of this method.
evidence: This is an observation based on literature review at the time of manuscript preparation.

claim: The limited practical use of prime editing might be due to the extensive optimization it requires and the relatively low editing efficiency that can be achieved at a subset of targets.
source: This might be due to the extensive optimization it requires and the relatively low editing efficiency that can be achieved at a subset of targets.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the limited adoption of prime editing.

claim: Any approach that can substantially increase the editing efficiency is critical to aid the generalized use of prime editing.
source: In this aspect, any approach that can substantially increase the editing efficiency is critical to aid its generalized use.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the importance of improving prime editing efficiency.

claim: Enrichment with a transfection marker resulted in only a 1.45-fold increment on average in all experiments, whilst PEAR enrichments tripled the number of edited cells.
source: In fact, enrichment with a transfection marker resulted in only a 1.45-fold increment on average in all experiments, whilst PEAR enrichments tripled the number of edited cells (Figures 3A, C ,, 4C).
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental data shown in Figures 3A, 3C, and 4C.

claim: The application of PEAR as a surrogate marker could substantially contribute to the more widespread use of prime editing by considerably increasing the number of potential targets which may now be edited with appropriate efficiency.
source: Thus, the application of PEAR as a surrogate marker, as demonstrated in four cell lines including HUES9 cells, could substantially contribute to the more widespread use of prime editing by considerably increasing the number of potential targets, which may now be edited with appropriate efficiency.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: PEAR is a versatile tool that can be utilized for the characterization of different prime editors.
source: PEAR is also a versatile tool that can be utilized for the characterization of different PEs.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing optimization of various parameters in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: More than 250 conditions combining different sgRNAs, PBS- and RT-lengths, and nick sites were examined using PEAR.
source: We examined more than 250 conditions combining different sgRNAs, PBS- and RT-lengths, and nick sites, and our results confirmed that the efficiency of prime editing to modify PEAR plasmids is governed by the same factors as prime editing in genomic context (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental work performed.

claim: The tolerance of the splice donor site for substitutions makes the target region sequence of the PEAR plasmid readily adjustable.
source: The tolerance of the splice donor site for substitutions (Figure 1D; Tálas et al., 2021) makes the target region sequence of the PEAR plasmid readily adjustable.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data in Figure 1D and citation to previous work.

claim: The versatility of PEAR allows the user to examine the effect of sequence features and other factors affecting the efficiency of prime editing in a systematic manner that cannot be explored otherwise using genomic targets.
source: This versatility allows the user to examine the effect of sequence features and other factors affecting the efficiency of prime editing in a systematic manner that cannot be explored otherwise using genomic targets.
evidence: This is an inference based on the demonstrated flexibility of PEAR.

claim: PEAR may assist the development of more efficient prime editors or variants with enhanced characteristics in the future.
source: Our approach, beyond its general use, may also assist the development of more efficient PEs or variants with enhanced characteristics in the future.
evidence: This is a speculation about future applications of PEAR.

claim: PEAR is expected to become a widespread tool to be used in a wide variety of biomedical and biotechnological applications.
source: Owning to the relatively low efficiency of prime editing with many potential target sequences, PEAR is expected to become a widespread tool to be used in a wide variety of biomedical and biotechnological applications.
evidence: This is a speculation about the future adoption of PEAR.

claim: PEAR may be an especially useful tool to be used with hard-to-edit cells or where the efficiency of prime editors is particularly compromised.
source: PEAR may be an especially useful tool to be used with hard-to-edit cells or where the efficiency of PEs is particularly compromised.
evidence: This is an inference based on the demonstrated enrichment capabilities of PEAR, particularly in HUES9 cells.

claim: HEK293T cells are very susceptible to prime editing due to the fact that their mismatch repair system is partially defective.
source: Since HEK293T cells are very susceptible to prime editing due to the fact that their mismatch repair system is partially defective (Chen et al., 2021; Trojan et al., 2002), we also attempted enrichment in K562 and U2OS cells, and on a human embryonic stem cell line HUES9, that are all less susceptible to prime editing (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: K562, U2OS, and HUES9 cells are all less susceptible to prime editing than HEK293T cells.
source: Since HEK293T cells are very susceptible to prime editing due to the fact that their mismatch repair system is partially defective (Chen et al., 2021; Trojan et al., 2002), we also attempted enrichment in K562 and U2OS cells, and on a human embryonic stem cell line HUES9, that are all less susceptible to prime editing (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3C-E.

claim: The editing rates increased using transfection marker enrichment by up to 1.65-fold.
source: The editing rates increased using transfection marker enrichment by up to 1.65-fold; however, they all showed a significantly greater increase when the PEAR enrichment was used.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: PEAR is based on the same concept as BEAR and contains the same inactive splice site.
source: The mechanism of PEAR is based on the same concept as BEAR (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B), and it contains the same inactive splice site, shown in (A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: PE can revert the 'G-AC-AAGT' sequence to the canonical 'G-GT-AAGT' splice site in PEAR.
source: PE can revert the 'G-AC-AAGT' sequence to the canonical 'G-GT-AAGT' splice site.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Prime editing occurs downstream of the cut site in the target.
source: Prime editing occurs downstream of the cut site in the target; hence, this method enables us to position the spacer sequence within the intron, thus, the entire length of the spacer (shown as 'N'-s) is freely adjustable in PEAR.
evidence: This is based on the known mechanism of prime editing and the design shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In the PEAR system, GFP fluorescence can be restored from various inactive splice sequences not only by substitutions but also by insertions/deletions.
source: In the PEAR system, GFP fluorescence can be restored from various inactive splice sequences not only by substitutions but also by insertions/deletions.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Prime editing can result in various active splice sequences, demonstrating the sequence flexibility of the PEAR system.
source: Prime editing can result in various active splice sequences, further demonstrating the sequence flexibility of the PEAR system.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Based on previous work, four additional active splice site variants were selected for testing in PEAR.
source: Based on Tálas et al., 2021, four additional active splice site variants were selected.
evidence: This is based on citation to previous work.

claim: To generate suitable inactive plasmids, splicing was disrupted by systematically replacing the 5′-GT splice donor site to 5′-AC and 5′-CT.
source: To generate suitable inactive plasmids, splicing was disrupted by systematically replacing the 5′-GT splice donor site to 5′-AC and 5′-CT (negative controls with inactive sequences, gray columns).
evidence: This describes the experimental design shown in Figure 1D.

claim: With the appropriate pegRNAs, PE2 was able to restore GFP fluorescence in every case of the four active splice site variants tested.
source: With the appropriate pegRNAs, PE2 was able to restore GFP fluorescence in every case (green columns).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1D.
